# The Lorentzian/Poisson kernel $\delta_n(x)=\dfrac n\pi\dfrac1{1+n^2x^2}$ is a delta sequence

## Statement

For each $n\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ define
$$\delta_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\qquad \delta_n(x):=\frac n\pi\,\frac1{1+n^2x^2}.$$
Then $\langle \delta_n\rangle_{n\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$ is a **delta sequence**: for every test function
$\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,\phi(x)\,dx=\phi(0)=\delta(\phi),$$
i.e. the regular distributions $T_{\delta_n}$ converge in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$ to the Dirac delta distribution $\delta$.

The formula "$\lim_{n\to\infty}\delta_n(x)=\delta(x)$" is an abuse of notation; the displayed limit of
integrals is the precise assertion, and it is what we prove. (See the Remark in §6: the pointwise
limit of $\delta_n$ is **not** $\delta$ in any functional sense, and the proof below is careful never
to interchange the pointwise limit with the integral.)

Throughout, $n$ denotes a **positive** integer, so $n>0$; integrals are Lebesgue integrals.

---

## 1. $\delta_n$ is well defined, continuous, positive, and measurable

For all real $x$ and all $n\ge 1$ we have $n^2x^2\ge 0$, hence
$$1+n^2x^2\ge 1>0 .$$
So the denominator never vanishes, $\delta_n$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and it is a quotient of
polynomials with non-vanishing denominator, hence **continuous** (therefore Borel measurable) on $\mathbb R$.
Moreover $n>0$ and $1+n^2x^2>0$ give
$$\delta_n(x)>0\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb R. \tag{1.1}$$

Finally, $\delta_n$ is bounded: since $1+n^2x^2\ge1$,
$$0<\delta_n(x)\le \frac n\pi\qquad (x\in\mathbb R). \tag{1.2}$$

---

## 2. Exact primitive and the mass of $\delta_n$ on a bounded interval

Define
$$F_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\qquad F_n(x):=\frac1\pi\arctan(nx).$$

**Lemma 2.1.** $F_n$ is continuously differentiable on $\mathbb R$ and $F_n'=\delta_n$.

*Proof.* The function $\arctan:\mathbb R\to(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$ is differentiable with
$\arctan'(t)=\dfrac1{1+t^2}$. (Indeed, $\tan$ is differentiable on $(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$ with
$\tan'(t)=1+\tan^2 t>0$, so it is a strictly increasing bijection onto $\mathbb R$; by the inverse
function theorem, for $u=\tan t$,
$\arctan'(u)=\frac1{\tan'(t)}=\frac1{1+\tan^2t}=\frac1{1+u^2}$.)
The map $x\mapsto nx$ is differentiable with derivative $n$, so by the chain rule
$$F_n'(x)=\frac1\pi\cdot\frac{1}{1+(nx)^2}\cdot n=\frac n\pi\,\frac1{1+n^2x^2}=\delta_n(x).$$
Since $\delta_n$ is continuous (§1), $F_n\in C^1(\mathbb R)$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.2 (mass on $[-a,a]$).** For every $a>0$ and every $n\ge1$,
$$\int_{-a}^{a}\delta_n(x)\,dx=\frac2\pi\arctan(na). \tag{2.1}$$

*Proof.* On the compact interval $[-a,a]$ the integrand $\delta_n$ is continuous, hence Riemann
integrable there, and its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree. By Lemma 2.1, $F_n$ is an
antiderivative of the *continuous* function $\delta_n$ on $[-a,a]$, so the Fundamental Theorem of
Calculus applies in its elementary form (no pathologies such as Volterra-type nowhere-Riemann-integrable
derivatives, or Cantor-function-type singular monotone functions, can occur here: the integrand is
continuous and the antiderivative is $C^1$ with derivative equal to it everywhere):
$$\int_{-a}^{a}\delta_n(x)\,dx=F_n(a)-F_n(-a)=\frac1\pi\bigl(\arctan(na)-\arctan(-na)\bigr)
=\frac2\pi\arctan(na),$$
using that $\arctan$ is odd. $\blacksquare$

*(Note: no change of variables is performed anywhere in this proof, so no Jacobian factor can be
misplaced. Formula (2.1) is obtained directly from an explicitly verified antiderivative.)*

**Corollary 2.3 (total mass $1$).**
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx=1\qquad\text{for every }n\ge1. \tag{2.2}$$
In particular $\delta_n\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ with $\|\delta_n\|_{L^1}=1$; hence $\delta_n$ is locally
integrable and defines a regular distribution $T_{\delta_n}$.

*Proof.* Put $g_k:=\delta_n\cdot\mathbf 1_{[-k,k]}$ for $k\in\mathbb N_{>0}$. By (1.1) each $g_k\ge0$, and
$g_k\le g_{k+1}$ pointwise, with $g_k\uparrow \delta_n$ pointwise as $k\to\infty$ (every $x$ lies in
$[-k,k]$ for $k$ large). The Monotone Convergence Theorem and (2.1) give
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n=\lim_{k\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}g_k=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac2\pi\arctan(nk)
=\frac2\pi\cdot\frac\pi2=1,$$
since $nk\to+\infty$ (here $n\ge1>0$ and $k\to+\infty$, so the product does tend to $+\infty$) and
$\arctan(t)\to\pi/2$ as $t\to+\infty$. $\blacksquare$

---

## 3. The tails of $\delta_n$ vanish uniformly away from the origin

**Lemma 3.1.** For every $a>0$ and every $n\ge1$,
$$\int_{\{|x|\ge a\}}\delta_n(x)\,dx\;\le\;\frac{2}{\pi n a}. \tag{3.1}$$
Consequently, for each **fixed** $a>0$, $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\{|x|\ge a\}}\delta_n(x)\,dx=0$.

*Proof.* For $|x|\ge a>0$ we have $x^2\ge a^2>0$ and $1+n^2x^2>n^2x^2>0$, hence
$$0<\delta_n(x)=\frac n\pi\cdot\frac1{1+n^2x^2}<\frac n\pi\cdot\frac1{n^2x^2}=\frac1{\pi n x^2}.$$
Therefore, using symmetry of the bound in $x\mapsto -x$ and the elementary computation
$\int_a^{\infty}x^{-2}dx=1/a$ (again by the FTC applied to the $C^1$ antiderivative $-1/x$ of the
continuous function $x^{-2}$ on $[a,R]$, followed by monotone convergence as $R\to\infty$):
$$\int_{\{|x|\ge a\}}\delta_n(x)\,dx\le \frac1{\pi n}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{-a}\frac{dx}{x^2}+\int_a^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2}\right)
=\frac1{\pi n}\cdot\frac2a=\frac2{\pi n a}.$$
With $a>0$ fixed, the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$. $\blacksquare$

*(Equivalently and exactly, by (2.1) and (2.2): $\int_{|x|>a}\delta_n=1-\frac2\pi\arctan(na)
=\frac2\pi\arctan\frac1{na}$. The explicit bound (3.1) is all we shall need, and it makes the rate
$O(1/n)$ visible.)*

---

## 4. The pairing $\langle T_{\delta_n},\phi\rangle$ is well defined

Let $\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$. Then $\phi$ is smooth — in particular continuous — and has compact
support $K=\operatorname{supp}\phi$. A continuous function on a compact set is bounded, and $\phi$
vanishes off $K$, so
$$M:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|\phi(x)|<\infty . \tag{4.1}$$
Also $\phi$ is continuous at $0$.

Since $\delta_n\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ (Corollary 2.3) and $\phi$ is bounded and measurable,
$|\delta_n\phi|\le M\,\delta_n\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, so $\delta_n\phi\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and
$$\left|\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n\phi\right|\le M .$$
Thus $\langle T_{\delta_n},\phi\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx$ is a well-defined real number.

Because $\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n=1$ by (2.2), the constant $\phi(0)$ can be absorbed into the integral:
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx-\phi(0)
=\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx-\phi(0)\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\,dx
=\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\bigl(\phi(x)-\phi(0)\bigr)\,dx, \tag{4.2}$$
the splitting being legitimate since both $\delta_n\phi$ and $\phi(0)\delta_n$ are in $L^1(\mathbb R)$
(linearity of the Lebesgue integral on $L^1$).

---

## 5. Proof of the theorem

**Theorem.** For every $\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$,
$\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx=\phi(0)$.

*Proof.* Let $\varepsilon>0$ be given, and let $M$ be as in (4.1).

**(i) Choice of $a$ (continuity at the origin).** Since $\phi$ is continuous at $0$, there is $a>0$ such that
$$|x|\le a\ \Longrightarrow\ |\phi(x)-\phi(0)|\le\frac\varepsilon2. \tag{5.1}$$
Fix such an $a$; note $a$ depends only on $\varepsilon$ and $\phi$, **not** on $n$.

**(ii) Splitting.** By (4.2) and the triangle inequality for integrals, splitting $\mathbb R$ into the
disjoint measurable sets $A:=\{|x|\le a\}$ and $B:=\{|x|>a\}$,
$$\left|\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n\phi-\phi(0)\right|
\le\underbrace{\int_{A}\delta_n(x)\,|\phi(x)-\phi(0)|\,dx}_{=:I_n}
+\underbrace{\int_{B}\delta_n(x)\,|\phi(x)-\phi(0)|\,dx}_{=:J_n},$$
where we used $\delta_n>0$ from (1.1).

**(iii) The central part.** By (5.1), on $A$ the integrand is at most $\tfrac\varepsilon2\delta_n(x)$, so by (2.2)
$$I_n\le\frac\varepsilon2\int_{A}\delta_n(x)\,dx\le\frac\varepsilon2\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\,dx=\frac\varepsilon2 .$$
This bound holds for **every** $n\ge1$.

**(iv) The tail part.** For all $x$, $|\phi(x)-\phi(0)|\le|\phi(x)|+|\phi(0)|\le 2M$ by (4.1). Hence by Lemma 3.1,
$$J_n\le 2M\int_{\{|x|>a\}}\delta_n(x)\,dx\le 2M\int_{\{|x|\ge a\}}\delta_n(x)\,dx\le\frac{4M}{\pi n a}.$$

**(v) Conclusion.** Combining (iii) and (iv), for every $n\ge1$,
$$\left|\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n\phi-\phi(0)\right|\le\frac\varepsilon2+\frac{4M}{\pi n a}. \tag{5.2}$$
If $M=0$ then $\phi\equiv0$ and the claim is trivial. Otherwise choose
$$N:=\left\lceil\frac{8M}{\pi a\varepsilon}\right\rceil+1,$$
so that for all $n\ge N$ we have $n>\dfrac{8M}{\pi a\varepsilon}$, i.e. $\dfrac{4M}{\pi n a}<\dfrac\varepsilon2$.
Then (5.2) yields
$$n\ge N\ \Longrightarrow\ \left|\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx-\phi(0)\right|<\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n\phi=\phi(0)=\delta(\phi)$.
$\blacksquare$

Since $\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)$ was arbitrary, $T_{\delta_n}\to\delta$ in the weak-$*$ topology of
$\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)$, which is exactly the assertion that $\langle\delta_n\rangle_{n\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$
is a delta sequence. $\qquad\blacksquare$

---

## 6. Remarks

**6.1 No illegitimate interchange of limit and integral.** For each fixed $x\ne 0$,
$$\delta_n(x)=\frac n\pi\,\frac1{1+n^2x^2}\le\frac n\pi\cdot\frac1{n^2x^2}=\frac1{\pi n x^2}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0,$$
while $\delta_n(0)=n/\pi\to+\infty$. So $\delta_n\to 0$ pointwise a.e., yet $\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n=1$
for every $n$. Passing the limit inside the integral would therefore give the false value $0$; this is
precisely the classical "escaping bump" failure of naive interchange (dominated convergence is
inapplicable: if a measurable $g$ satisfied $g\ge\delta_n$ for all $n$, then for $0<|x|\le\frac12$ the
choice $n=\lfloor 1/|x|\rfloor$ gives $n\ge 1$, $n|x|\le1$ — hence $1+n^2x^2\le2$ — and
$n\ge\frac1{|x|}-1\ge\frac1{2|x|}$, so
$g(x)\ge\delta_n(x)\ge\frac{n}{2\pi}\ge\frac1{4\pi|x|}$, which is not integrable near $0$). The proof in §5 never performs such an interchange:
it uses only the exact identity $\int\delta_n=1$, the continuity of $\phi$ at $0$, and the quantitative
tail bound (3.1). This is also why the limit function $\delta$ cannot be an ordinary function and must be
understood as a distribution.

**6.2 Alternative ending via dominated convergence (done correctly).** One may instead substitute
$x=u/n$ (so $dx=du/n$, and the factor $n/\pi$ cancels the $1/n$, leaving $\frac1\pi\frac{du}{1+u^2}$ —
the Jacobian appears in the numerator here) to get from (4.2)
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n\phi-\phi(0)=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\phi(u/n)-\phi(0)}{1+u^2}\,du .$$
Now the integrand converges to $0$ for **every** $u$ (continuity of $\phi$ at $0$ and $u/n\to0$), and it
is dominated for all $n$ by the single integrable function $u\mapsto \frac{2M}{\pi(1+u^2)}$, whose
integral is $2M$. Dominated convergence — whose hypotheses are genuinely verified here, unlike in 6.1 —
gives limit $0$. We presented §5 as the main argument because it is elementary, quantitative, and
independent of any change-of-variables bookkeeping.

**6.3 Rate and generality.** Estimate (5.2) shows the convergence is $O(1/n)$ in general (the heavy
$x^{-2}$ tails of the Lorentzian prevent a faster universal rate). Note also that the argument used
only that $\phi$ is **bounded, measurable, and continuous at $0$**; smoothness and compact support were
never needed. Hence the same conclusion holds for every bounded continuous $\phi$ on $\mathbb R$ — in
particular, $\delta_n$ is the Poisson kernel for the upper half-plane at height $1/n$, and the theorem
is the statement that the Poisson integral of a bounded continuous function attains its boundary value
at $0$.
